doctrines/mary-saints/question: What honour is due to Mary, the mother of Jesus, and to the saints — and may Christians ask for their prayers and venerate their images?
doctrines/mary-saints/summary: From the early ‘new Eve’ typology and the cult of the martyrs, devotion to Mary and the saints grew into a central feature of Christian life. The Council of Ephesus (431) called Mary Theotokos (‘God-bearer’) to safeguard the unity of Christ. Perpetual virginity became the common belief of East and West; the Immaculate Conception (1854) and Assumption (1950) were defined as Catholic dogmas, while the Orthodox celebrate the Dormition. The iconoclast controversy ended with the Second Council of Nicaea (787) approving the veneration of icons. The Reformers rejected the invocation of saints and (in the Reformed tradition) religious images, while generally keeping Theotokos and often perpetual virginity. Today Marian devotion is among the most global features of Christianity, and a frequent subject of ecumenical dialogue.
doctrines/mary-saints/longText:
The New Testament presents Mary as the virgin mother of Jesus (Matthew 1; Luke 1–2), the ‘favoured one’ whom ‘all generations shall call blessed’ (Luke 1:28, 48), present at the cross (John 19:25–27) and among the disciples at Pentecost (Acts 1:14). Second-century writers developed a typology of Mary as the new Eve whose obedience undid Eve's disobedience (Justin, Irenaeus). The Protoevangelium of James (c. 150) narrated Mary's own birth and virginal purity, shaping later belief and feasts. Alongside, Christians honoured martyrs: the Martyrdom of Polycarp (c. 155) describes the gathering of his bones and the annual celebration of his ‘birthday’ into heaven. By the fourth century, shrines, relics, pilgrimage and requests for saints' prayers were widespread across the Mediterranean, Syria, Egypt and beyond (Peter Brown).

The title Theotokos (‘God-bearer’) appears in Alexandrian usage from the third or fourth century and in the early prayer Sub tuum praesidium. When Nestorius preferred ‘Christotokos’, the Council of Ephesus (431) affirmed Theotokos — fundamentally a statement about Christ: the one born of Mary is God the Word incarnate. Mary's perpetual virginity was defended by Jerome against Helvidius (383), who held that the ‘brothers of Jesus’ were Mary's later children; the title Aeiparthenos (‘ever-virgin’) was used at Constantinople II (553). Feasts of the Annunciation and the Dormition spread; Emperor Maurice fixed the Dormition on 15 August (c. 600).

The veneration of images became a crisis when Byzantine emperors Leo III (from c. 726–730) and Constantine V (Council of Hieria, 754) banned and destroyed icons as idolatrous. John of Damascus argued that because God became visible in the flesh, he may be depicted, and that the honour given to an image passes to its prototype (Basil). The Second Council of Nicaea (787) distinguished worship (latreia), due to God alone, from honourable veneration (proskynesis) of icons. After a second iconoclast period, icons were restored in 843 — still celebrated in the Orthodox ‘Triumph of Orthodoxy’. Western reception was hesitant (Libri Carolini), but images and relics flourished in medieval Latin Christianity.

In the medieval West, theologians debated whether Mary was conceived free of original sin. Bernard of Clairvaux and Thomas Aquinas held that she was sanctified after conception; Duns Scotus argued that Christ, as perfect redeemer, preserved her from sin in advance. The feast of the Conception spread, and in 1854 Pius IX defined the Immaculate Conception in Ineffabilis Deus; in 1950 Pius XII defined the bodily Assumption in Munificentissimus Deus. The Orthodox venerate Mary as all-holy (Panagia) and celebrate her Dormition and translation to heaven, but most reject the Immaculate Conception as unnecessary and tied to an Augustinian doctrine of inherited guilt, and question the authority behind the definitions.

The Reformers retained deep respect for Mary: Luther and Zwingli affirmed Theotokos and perpetual virginity, and Luther wrote a warm commentary on the Magnificat (1521). But they rejected the invocation of saints as without scriptural warrant and as compromising Christ's sole mediation (1 Timothy 2:5), along with relics, pilgrimages and indulgences. The Reformed tradition went further, removing images from churches as violations of the second commandment, sometimes through violent iconoclasm (Zürich 1524; the Netherlands 1566). The Council of Trent (1563) reaffirmed invocation of saints and veneration of images, while condemning abuses.

Vatican II (Lumen Gentium, 1964, chapter 8) placed Mary within the doctrine of the Church as its pre-eminent member and model, cautioning against both exaggeration and neglect. Marian devotion is especially strong in Latin America (Our Lady of Guadalupe, 1531), the Philippines, India, Poland, Ethiopia and the Oriental Orthodox churches; approved apparitions (Lourdes 1858, Fatima 1917, Kibeho 1981) attract millions. Ecumenical agreed statements (Lutheran–Catholic 1990; ARCIC 2005) have found significant convergence on Mary's place in the economy of salvation, while differences remain over the dogmas, the invocation of saints, and proposed titles such as ‘Co-redemptrix’.
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/0/label: What honour is due to Mary and the saints — and may we ask their prayers and venerate their images?
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/0/text: Questions about Mary are always also questions about Christ, about the communion of saints, and about the second commandment.
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/1/label: Exod 20:4–5 — ‘Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image’
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/1/text: The second commandment: for iconoclasts and the Reformed, a ban on religious images in worship; for iconodules, a ban on idols that the incarnation transformed (cf. the cherubim of Exodus 25:18–22).
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/2/label: Luke 1:28–48 — ‘full of grace’; ‘all generations shall call me blessed’
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/2/text: The Annunciation and Magnificat: foundational for every Marian theology (Greek kecharitomene, ‘highly favoured’).
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/3/label: Matt 1:25; Mark 6:3 — ‘till she had brought forth’; ‘his brethren’
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/3/text: Read as evidence for Mary's later children (Helvidian view) or as cousins/step-siblings (Jerome; Epiphanius).
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/4/text: Jesus entrusts Mary to the beloved disciple; read as Mary's spiritual motherhood of believers.
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/5/label: Rev 12:1–6 — ‘a woman clothed with the sun’
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/5/text: Read of Israel, the Church and (from the 4th century especially) of Mary, glorified.
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/6/label: Heb 12:1; Rev 5:8; 6:9–10 — ‘so great a cloud of witnesses’
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/6/text: The departed saints are alive, aware and praying: the basis for intercession of saints.
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/7/label: 1 Tim 2:5 — ‘one mediator between God and men’
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/7/text: The Reformers' key text against invoking saints; Catholics and Orthodox read it as compatible with subordinate intercession (cf. 1 Timothy 2:1).
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/8/label: Protoevangelium of James: Mary's birth and virginity
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/8/text: Mary's parents Joachim and Anne; Joseph as an elderly widower with children — shaping the Eastern view of Jesus' ‘brothers’.
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/9/label: Justin and Irenaeus: Mary the new Eve
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/9/text: Mary's obedient faith unties the knot of Eve's disobedience.
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/10/labe: The cult of the martyrs: Polycarp's relics
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/10/text: The Smyrnaeans gather Polycarp's bones and keep the anniversary of his martyrdom — the seed of the cult of saints.
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/11/labe: Ephrem the Syrian: hymns to the spotless Mother
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/11/text: Syriac poetry celebrating Mary's purity and the paradox of the Virgin Mother.
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/12/labe: Basil: the honour of the image passes to the prototype
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/12/text: A Trinitarian analogy later used as the key principle of icon theology.
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/13/text: Jerome replies with Against Helvidius, defending perpetual virginity.
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/14/text: Common teaching of East and West; title used at Constantinople II (553).
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/15/text: Mary bore the man in whom the Word dwelt.
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/16/labe: Council of Ephesus: Mary is Theotokos
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/16/text: The people of Ephesus reportedly celebrated with torchlight processions.
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/17/text: A Christological title that becomes the heart of Marian devotion.
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/18/labe: Marian feasts and the Dormition (15 August)
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/18/text: Dormition narratives circulate from the late 5th century; Emperor Maurice fixes the feast c. 600.
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/19/text: Leo III and Constantine V (Hieria 754): icons are idols; only the Eucharist is the true image of Christ.
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/20/labe: John of Damascus: God became matter; he may be depicted
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/20/text: From Muslim-ruled Palestine (Mar Saba), John defends icons on incarnational grounds.
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/21/labe: Second Council of Nicaea: veneration, not worship
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/21/text: Icons receive honourable veneration (proskynesis); worship (latreia) belongs to God alone.
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/22/text: Restored under Empress Theodora (843): the ‘Triumph of Orthodoxy’.
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/23/labe: Bernard and Aquinas: Mary sanctified after conception
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/23/text: Mary was cleansed in the womb, but not conceived without original sin — otherwise she would not need Christ's redemption.
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/24/text: Christ redeemed Mary most perfectly by preserving her from original sin.
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/25/text: Invocation of saints rejected (Augsburg Confession 21; Smalcald Articles); Reformed iconoclasm (Zürich 1524, Geneva, Netherlands 1566).
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/26/text: The reported apparition to Juan Diego near Mexico City becomes the centre of Mexican and Latin American Catholic identity; the basilica is among the world's most visited shrines.
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/27/labe: Trent: invocation of saints and images reaffirmed
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/27/text: Session XXV: it is good and useful to invoke the saints; images are honoured for what they represent; abuses condemned.
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/28/text: Pius IX defines the dogma after consulting the world's bishops; Lourdes (1858) follows.
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/29/text: Pius XII's only ex cathedra definition; the question of whether Mary died is left open.
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/30/labe: Vatican II: Mary within the mystery of the Church
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/30/text: Lumen Gentium ch. 8 instead of a separate Marian document; Mary as type and mother of the Church.
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/31/labe: Ecumenical agreed statements on Mary and the saints
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/31/text: Lutheran–Catholic ‘The One Mediator, the Saints, and Mary’ (1990); Groupe des Dombes (1997–98); ARCIC ‘Mary: Grace and Hope in Christ’ (2005).
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/32/text: Millions of signatures since the 1990s sought a fifth Marian dogma; popes declined, and in 2025 a doctrinal note of the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith judged the title inappropriate.
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/33/labe: Today: global Marian devotion, diverse convictions
doctrines/mary-saints/flow/nodes/33/text: Catholic, Orthodox and Oriental churches (especially Ethiopia, Egypt, India, Latin America, the Philippines) practise intensive devotion to Mary and the saints; most Protestants honour Mary as a model of faith without invocation.
doctrines/ethics-church-state/question: How should Christians relate to political power, violence and injustice?
doctrines/ethics-church-state/summary: From Tertullian’s refusal of the sword to Constantine’s Christian empire, Luther’s two kingdoms, Anabaptist separation, the slavery debates, the Social Gospel, Barmen, liberation theology and today’s Christian nationalism, Christians have continually renegotiated their relation to power, war and justice.
doctrines/ethics-church-state/longText:
The earliest Christians were a persecuted minority who prayed for emperors but refused to worship them. Jesus’ command to love enemies and his rebuke of Peter’s sword led most pre-Constantinian writers, such as Tertullian and Origen, to oppose Christians killing in war, even as Christians increasingly served in the army. Paul’s instruction that rulers are "ministers of God" bearing the sword, and Jesus’ "render unto Caesar", supplied the other pole of the tension.

Constantine’s conversion (312) transformed the question. Eusebius hailed a Christian empire, Theodosius made Nicene Christianity the state religion (380), and Byzantium developed the ideal of "symphony" between emperor and patriarch, a pattern echoed in Russia, Ethiopia and Armenia. Augustine, writing after the sack of Rome, relativised every earthly city while articulating the principles of justified war that Aquinas, Vitoria and Grotius later systematised. In the West, Pope Gelasius’ "two powers" grounded the medieval contest between popes and emperors. Christendom produced hospitals, universities and law, but also crusades, inquisitions and conquests whose injustices critics like Bartolomé de las Casas denounced.

The Reformation multiplied models. Luther taught two kingdoms; Calvin a twofold government in which the magistrate upheld true religion; Anabaptists at Schleitheim (1527) renounced the sword and magistracy and were persecuted by all. Wars of religion led, slowly, to toleration and in America to the separation of church and state. In the 18th and 19th centuries Christians stood on both sides of the greatest moral question of the age: Quakers, evangelicals, Methodists and Black Christians led the abolition of slavery while Southern theologians defended it from Scripture, splitting the American churches.

In the industrial age the Social Gospel and Catholic social teaching called for justice for workers. Under Nazism the Confessing Church’s Barmen Declaration (1934) confessed Christ’s sole lordship against the "German Christians"; Martin Luther King Jr. drew on the Black church, the Social Gospel and natural law in the civil rights struggle; Latin American bishops and theologians such as Gustavo Gutiérrez proclaimed a preferential option for the poor; South African churches declared apartheid theology a heresy. Today churches debate nuclear weapons and humanitarian intervention, religious liberty, persecution, and the resurgence of Christian nationalism from the United States to Russia. This section presents each tradition’s case in its own terms, including a critical historical account of pro-slavery theology, together with its strongest critics.
doctrines/ethics-church-state/flow/nodes: How should Christians relate to political power, violence and injustice?

Jesus told Peter to put away his sword and said "my kingdom is not of this world", yet Paul calls the ruler "the minister of God" who "beareth not the sword in vain". May Christians kill in war or hold office? Should the Church be allied to the state, separate from it, or prophetically against it? How did Christians justify, and then overthrow, slavery? What is the Church’s responsibility for the poor and oppressed?
Sermon on the Mount and the sword (Matthew 5:38–48; 26:52; John 18:36)
"Resist not evil ... love your enemies"; "all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword". Pacifists read these as binding on all disciples; others limit them to personal ethics.
Caesar and God (Mark 12:17; Acts 5:29)
"Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s"; "we ought to obey God rather than men". The basis for both loyalty and resistance.
Romans 13:1–7 and 1 Peter 2:13–17: the governing authorities
Rulers are ordained by God, bear the sword to punish evildoers and must be obeyed for conscience’ sake; contrast Revelation 13, where imperial power appears as a beast.
Slavery texts (Exodus 21; Leviticus 25:44–46; Ephesians 6:5–9; Philemon; Galatians 3:28; 1 Timothy 1:10)

The Bible regulates slavery, the household codes command slaves to obey, and Paul returns Onesimus "not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved", while condemning "menstealers" and declaring "neither bond nor free" in Christ. Both sides of the 19th-century debate quoted these texts.
Tertullian and Origen: Christians do not fight

Pre-Constantinian writers generally oppose Christians killing in war and serving as magistrates, partly over bloodshed and partly over idolatrous military oaths; Christians nonetheless served in the army by the late 2nd century.
Christian pacifism and nonviolence
Followers of Jesus renounce lethal violence and overcome evil with good.
Constantine: "Conquer by this" (312)
After his victory at the Milvian Bridge, Constantine favours the Church; the Edict of Milan (313) grants toleration and Eusebius hails a Christian empire.
The Constantinian synthesis (Christendom)
Church and empire cooperate as two arms of one Christian society: emperors convene councils and enforce orthodoxy; bishops pray for and legitimise rulers.
Edict of Thessalonica makes Nicene Christianity the state religion (380)
Theodosius I’s edict Cunctos populos (380) requires all subjects to hold the faith of the bishops of Rome and Alexandria; pagan sacrifice is banned in 391–92. Heresy becomes a crime.
Augustine: two cities, and war as tragic necessity
After the sack of Rome (410) Augustine relativises every earthly state as the "earthly city" while arguing that rulers may wage war to restrain evil, with love rather than hatred as the motive.
Just war tradition
War may be justified as a last resort to restrain grave evil, under criteria of authority, cause, intention and restraint.
Gelasius: "two there are" by which the world is ruled (494)

Against imperial interference, the pope distinguishes priestly authority from royal power, the seed of medieval papal claims (Unam Sanctam, 1302) and of later church–state distinctions. Byzantium meanwhile develops Justinian’s ideal of "symphony" between emperor and patriarch (Novel 6, 535).
Aquinas systematises just war (c.1272)
Legitimate authority, just cause and right intention; later scholastics (Vitoria, Suárez) and Grotius extend it into international law.
Valladolid debate on the conquest of the Americas (1550–51)

Charles V convenes Las Casas and Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda to debate whether war and subjugation of indigenous Americans are just. No formal verdict was issued, but the debate fed the New Laws (1542) and the development of natural rights theory.
Lutheran two kingdoms
God rules the world through the sword of temporal government and the Church through the gospel; Christians serve in both.
Anabaptist separation and nonresistance
The Schleitheim brethren separate from the world, renounce the sword, oath and magistracy, and form disciplined believers’ churches.
Augsburg Confession XVI: Christians may bear office and fight just wars (1530)

Lutheran, Reformed (e.g. Belgic Confession 36) and Anglican (Article XXXVII) confessions affirm magistracy and just war and condemn the Anabaptists; thousands of Anabaptists are executed by Catholic and Protestant authorities alike.
Confessional states and wars of religion (1555–1648)

The Peace of Augsburg (1555) lets each prince choose his territory’s religion; religious wars culminate in the Thirty Years’ War, ended by the Peace of Westphalia (1648). Exhaustion with religious violence helps birth arguments for toleration (Roger Williams, Locke) and later the separation of church and state.
Quaker Peace Testimony (1661)
Quakers join Mennonites and Brethren as the historic "peace churches"; they will also lead early abolitionism (Germantown Protest, 1688; John Woolman; Anthony Benezet).
Christian abolitionism
Quakers, evangelicals (Wilberforce, the Clapham Sect), Methodists and Black churches campaign against the slave trade and slavery as sins against the image of God.
Britain abolishes the slave trade (1807)
After twenty years of evangelical and Quaker campaigning, Parliament bans the trade; slavery itself is abolished in British colonies from 1834, in the US in 1865 and in Brazil in 1888.
Pro-slavery theology (historical)
Southern US theologians argue that Scripture sanctions slavery; here described historically and critically, as now repudiated by virtually all churches.
Churches split over slavery (1844–61) and the Civil War

The Methodist Episcopal Church (1844), Baptists (Southern Baptist Convention, 1845) and Presbyterians (1857, 1861) divide North and South; Mark Noll calls the Civil War a "theological crisis" because both sides read the same Bible to opposite conclusions. The SBC formally apologised for its defence of slavery and racism in 1995.
The Social Gospel
Walter Rauschenbusch and others call the Church to Christianise the social order in the face of industrial poverty.
Barmen Declaration (1934)
The Confessing Church rejects the Nazi-aligned "German Christians" and any lordship besides Christ; Dietrich Bonhoeffer later joins the conspiracy against Hitler and is executed in April 1945.
Martin Luther King Jr.: nonviolent resistance to unjust laws (1963)
The Black church fuses Social Gospel, natural-law reasoning and Gandhian nonviolence in the civil rights movement.
Medellín: the Latin American bishops opt for the poor (1968)
CELAM’s Medellín conference applies Vatican II to Latin America, denouncing "institutionalised violence" and calling for liberation; Puebla (1979) speaks of a "preferential option for the poor".
Liberation theology
Gutiérrez, Boff, Sobrino, Míguez Bonino; Black, Minjung, Dalit, Palestinian and feminist theologies; base ecclesial communities; martyrs such as Archbishop Óscar Romero (1980).
Objection: Vatican Instruction on liberation theology (1984)

The Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith under Cardinal Ratzinger warns against uncritical use of Marxist class analysis and reducing salvation to politics (Libertatis Nuntius, 1984), while affirming liberation as a Christian theme (Libertatis Conscientia, 1986). Under Pope Francis relations warmed; Gutiérrez was received at the Vatican and died in 2024.
Christian nationalism debates
Should a nation be self-consciously Christian in law and identity? Debated in the US, Russia ("Russian World"), Hungary, Brazil, Nigeria and elsewhere.
Global South: prophetic resistance and new alliances

South Africa’s Kairos Document (1985) and the Belhar Confession (1986) declare apartheid theology a heresy; churches in the Philippines (1986), Kenya, Zambia and DR Congo play roles in democratisation; persecution of Christians in North Korea, China and parts of the Middle East and Africa raises new questions of church–state relations.
Today: who holds what?

Just war is the mainstream teaching of Catholic, Orthodox (as "necessary evil" rather than a formal theory), Lutheran, Reformed and Anglican churches, though Pope Francis (Fratelli Tutti, 2020) questioned whether any modern war can meet its criteria. Mennonites, Quakers and Brethren maintain pacifism, joined by many Catholic and evangelical peace activists. Most churches accept religious liberty and some separation of church and state; established churches survive in England, Denmark and elsewhere. All major churches now condemn slavery and racism. Liberation and social-justice themes are widespread in Catholic social teaching and Global South theology, while debates over Christian nationalism are intensifying.
